cg.cg-intro.explain:
- Computer Graphics is the sub-field of computer science concerned with generating, manipulating, and rendering images and visual content using computers.
- It matters because visual communication is intuitive; it powers modern video games, CAD software for engineering design, scientific data visualization, and graphical user interfaces (GUIs).
- **Real-Life Analogy**: Imagine an artist painting on a digital canvas where the computer acts as both the brush and the physics engine, calculating light, shadow, and geometry in real time.
how: Define the geometric model of an object using vertices, edges, and polygons in coordinate space.
Apply transformations (translation, rotation, scaling) to position objects within the scene.
Perform projection to convert 3D coordinates onto a 2D viewing plane.
Rasterize vector primitives into discrete pixels on a frame buffer.
Apply shading, lighting, and texture mapping for realistic visual appearance.
Display the final pixel array onto a computer monitor at high refresh rates.
keyPoints: Computer Graphics bridges mathematical coordinates and visual human perception.
Divided into interactive graphics (user controls view) and non-interactive/rendering (offline CGI movies).
Primitives are basic geometric building blocks like points, lines, and polygons.
Rasterization is the process of converting geometric shapes into pixelated images.
Fundamental applications include CAD/CAM, Virtual Reality (VR), UI design, and video games.
mistakes: Confusing vector graphics with raster graphics -> Vector uses mathematical formulas (scalable without loss), raster uses grids of pixels.
Ignoring the coordinate system transformations -> Forgetting that objects must pass from modeling to world to viewing to projection coordinates.
theory: What is Computer Graphics?
It is the art and science of generating and manipulating images and visual data using computers.
What are graphics primitives?
Basic geometric elements used to construct digital images, such as points, lines, circles, and polygons.
What is the difference between Interactive and Non-Interactive Computer Graphics?
Interactive graphics allow user input to dynamically alter the scene (e.g., video games); non-interactive graphics are pre-rendered (e.g., CGI animation movies).
What is CAD used for?
Computer-Aided Design is used by engineers and architects to create precision drawings and 3D models.
Why is rasterization necessary?
Because standard computer displays are made of a discrete grid of pixels that cannot directly render continuous mathematical lines.

cg.cg-hardware.explain:
- Graphics hardware and software form the physical and programmatic foundation for rendering visual scenes.
- Hardware includes the **GPU** (Graphics Processing Unit), **Frame Buffer** (memory holding pixel colors), and displays (CRT, LCD, OLED). Software includes graphics APIs like **OpenGL**, **Vulkan**, and **WebGL**.
- It matters because real-time 3D rendering requires massive parallel computation that standard CPUs cannot handle efficiently.
- **Real-Life Analogy**: The CPU is like a master chef handling complex multi-step recipes, while the GPU is an army of line cooks chopping thousands of vegetables simultaneously.
how: CPU sends geometric data and draw commands to the GPU over the system bus.
GPU vertex shader processes object vertices in parallel.
Rasterizer converts primitives into fragments (potential pixels).
GPU fragment shader calculates lighting, color, and textures for each fragment.
Pixels are written into the Frame Buffer memory region.
Display controller refreshes the physical screen from the frame buffer contents.
keyPoints: Frame Buffer is a video RAM region that stores the color value of every pixel on the screen.
GPU features massively parallel architecture optimized for floating-point matrix operations.
OpenGL is a cross-language, cross-platform API for rendering 2D and 3D vector graphics.
WebGL brings OpenGL ES to web browsers via HTML5 Canvas without plugins.
CRT monitors used electron beams, whereas modern displays use flat-panel LCD/OLED matrices.
mistakes: Confusing CPU and GPU roles -> CPU handles general logic and scene graphs; GPU handles parallel geometry and pixel shading.
Writing direct hardware calls in modern applications -> Always use standard graphics APIs (OpenGL/Vulkan) or abstraction layers for portability.
theory: What is a Frame Buffer?
A portion of video RAM that stores the intensity/color values for every pixel displayed on a monitor screen.
Why are GPUs faster than CPUs for graphics?
GPUs have thousands of smaller, specialized cores designed for parallel processing of mathematical and matrix operations.
What is the role of OpenGL?
It is an industry-standard software interface (API) that allows programmers to interact with graphics hardware to render 2D and 3D graphics.
What is WebGL?
A JavaScript API based on OpenGL ES that enables high-performance interactive 2D and 3D graphics within any compatible web browser.
What is rasterization hardware acceleration?
Dedicated hardware circuitry inside the GPU designed to convert vector primitives into pixel fragments efficiently.

cg.points-lines.explain:
Points and lines are the fundamental geometric building blocks in Computer Graphics. A point represents a single coordinate position $(x, y)$ on a display screen, while a line connects two points $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$. Because screens are made of discrete pixels rather than continuous mathematical planes, drawing these primitives requires mapping continuous coordinates to discrete grid cells.

These primitives matter because every complex 3D model, UI window, and video game graphic is ultimately broken down into millions of tiny points and line segments. Without reliable pixel-level primitives, no shape or rendering pipeline could function.

Think of points and lines like a giant mosaic or cross-stitch pattern. Even though you want to draw a smooth diagonal line, you must figure out which individual square tiles (pixels) to paint to give the illusion of a continuous line.
how: Define the coordinate system (Cartesian or screen space with origin at top-left).
Map continuous floating-point or integer coordinates to integer screen pixel locations.
Use setPixel(x, y) functions to illuminate individual pixels for points.
Calculate intermediate pixel locations between two endpoints to draw lines.
keyPoints: Points are zero-dimensional primitives defined by $(x, y)$ coordinates.
Lines are one-dimensional primitives defined by start and end points.
Screen space typically has the origin $(0,0)$ at the top-left corner, unlike Cartesian coordinates.
Alias artifacts (jaggies) occur due to the discrete nature of pixel grids.
Rasterization is the process of converting geometric primitives into pixel representation.
mistakes: Confusing screen coordinate system $(0,0$ at top-left) with standard Cartesian coordinates ($0,0$ at bottom-left). Fix: Always invert the y-axis when mapping mathematical models to screen buffers.
Assuming lines can be drawn with infinite thinness without considering pixel width and height. Fix: Account for pixel centers during rasterization.
theory: What is a graphics primitive?
Basic geometric shapes like points, lines, and polygons used to construct more complex images.
Why do we need rasterization?
To convert continuous mathematical vector descriptions into discrete pixel intensities on a computer screen.
What causes 'jaggies' (aliasing)?
The stair-step effect visible on diagonal lines due to low-resolution discrete pixel grids.
How is screen coordinate system different from Cartesian?
Screen coordinates start with $(0,0)$ at the top-left, where $x$ increases right and $y$ increases down.
What is the fundamental unit of a computer display?
A pixel (picture element).

cg.dda.explain:
The Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) is a scan-conversion line drawing algorithm based on calculating either $\Delta x$ or $\Delta y$. It uses floating-point arithmetic to find the incremental steps needed to move from the starting pixel to the ending pixel. Depending on the slope of the line ($|m| \le 1$ or $|m| > 1$), it steps through one coordinate by unit increments (1 pixel) and calculates the corresponding fractional increments for the other coordinate, rounding to the nearest integer.

It matters in computer graphics as one of the earliest algorithmic approaches to rasterization, bridging the gap between analytical geometry and computer hardware.

Imagine walking up a staircase where the slope is constant. Instead of recalculating your height from the ground at every single step, you take a fixed step forward and add a small, constant rise to your current height.
how: Input the two endpoints of the line: $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$.
Calculate $\Delta x = x_2 - x_1$ and $\Delta y = y_2 - y_1$.
Determine the number of steps required: $steps = \max(|\Delta x|, |\Delta y|)$.
Calculate the increment per step: $xinc = \Delta x / steps$ and $yinc = \Delta y / steps$.
Loop `steps` times, rounding current $x$ and $y$ values to plot pixels.
keyPoints: DDA stands for Digital Differential Analyzer.
It uses floating-point calculations and rounding operations at each step.
Computationally slow because floating-point addition and rounding are expensive operations.
Prone to rounding errors accumulating over long lines.
Best suited for educational understanding rather than high-performance hardware rendering.
mistakes: Forgetting to handle vertical lines where $\Delta x = 0$, leading to division by zero. Fix: Add a check for $\Delta x == 0$ before computing increments.
Using integer division instead of floating-point division for increments. Fix: Cast $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$ to float before dividing.
theory: What is the main drawback of the DDA algorithm?
It uses slow floating-point arithmetic and rounding operations at every step.
How are steps calculated in DDA?
By finding the maximum absolute difference between $x$ coordinates or $y$ coordinates ($\max(|\Delta x|, |\Delta y|)$).
Does DDA work for all slopes?
Yes, by handling cases where $|m| \le 1$ and $|m| > 1$ differently.
What causes cumulative error in DDA?
Repeated rounding of floating-point numbers over long lines can cause drift.
What is the time complexity of DDA for a line of length $L$?
$O(L)$ where $L$ is the number of pixels.

Medium

cg.bresenham-line.explain:
Bresenham's Line Algorithm is an efficient rasterization method that determines which pixels should be plotted to form a close approximation to a straight line. Unlike DDA, Bresenham's algorithm uses **only integer addition, subtraction, and bit shifting**, completely avoiding slow floating-point division and rounding operations. It maintains a running decision parameter that tells the algorithm whether to step diagonally or straight along the primary axis.

It matters immensely in computer graphics and game engine development because execution speed is critical when drawing thousands of primitives per frame.

Imagine driving a car along a winding road where you only check whether you are closer to the left lane marker or right lane marker using simple integer tallies, avoiding complex GPS float calculations.
how: Input the two endpoints $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$, ensuring $x_1 < x_2$.
Calculate $\Delta x = x_2 - x_1$ and $\Delta y = y_2 - y_1$.
Initialize the decision parameter: $P_0 = 2\Delta y - \Delta x$.
For each $x$ along the line, if $P_k < 0$, the next point is $(x_k + 1, y_k)$ and $P_{k+1} = P_k + 2\Delta y$.
If $P_k \ge 0$, the next point is $(x_k + 1, y_k + 1)$ and $P_{k+1} = P_k + 2\Delta y - 2\Delta x$.
keyPoints: Uses exclusively fast integer arithmetic (no floating-point operations).
Significantly faster than the DDA line algorithm.
Decision parameter $P$ guides pixel selection dynamically.
Eliminates accumulation of rounding errors.
Standard algorithm taught in graphics and implemented in hardware/software renderers.
mistakes: Forgetting to multiply initial terms by 2, leading to incorrect decision parameter thresholds. Fix: Ensure initial $P = 2\Delta y - \Delta x$ and updates use $2\Delta y$ / $2\Delta x$.
Not swapping endpoints when $x_1 > x_2$. Fix: Implement proper boundary checks or swap logic at the start.
theory: Why is Bresenham's algorithm faster than DDA?
It uses only integer addition, subtraction, and multiplication by 2, avoiding floating-point division entirely.
What is the role of the decision parameter $P$?
It determines whether the next pixel should be plotted straight or diagonally by measuring the distance error.
Can Bresenham's algorithm handle all quadrants/slopes?
Yes, by adjusting sign increments and swapping axes for steep slopes ($|m| > 1$).
Who invented Bresenham's algorithm?
Jack E. Bresenham in 1962 at IBM.
What is the initialization formula for the decision parameter in the 1st octant?
$P_0 = 2\Delta y - \Delta x$.

cg.circle-polar.explain:
The polar coordinate method for drawing a circle relies on the trigonometric equations `x = x_c + r \cos(\theta)` and `y = y_c + r \sin(\theta)`, where `(x_c, y_c)` is the center of the circle, `r` is the radius, and `\theta` is the angle.

As `\theta` varies from `0` to `2\pi` (or `0` to `360^\circ`), the calculated floating-point coordinates trace out the circumference of a circle. Because we are plotting pixels on a discrete grid, these calculated floating-point values are rounded to the nearest integer.

This matters in computer graphics as a fundamental, intuitive approach to generating curved shapes, though it is computationally expensive due to repeated floating-point multiplication and trigonometric function calls (`\sin`, `\cos`).

Think of it like a clock hand of fixed length `r` pinned at a center point: as the angle `\theta` sweeps around the clock face, the tip of the hand traces out the circle's path.
how: Define the circle's center coordinates (xc, yc) and radius r.
Set an angular step size (e.g., d_theta = 1.0 / r or 1/r radians) to ensure no gaps between plotted pixels.
Loop theta from 0.0 up to 2 * PI using the chosen step size.
Calculate x = xc + r * cos(theta) and y = yc + r * sin(theta).
Round x and y to the nearest integer and plot the pixel at (round(x), round(y)).
Utilize 8-way symmetry to mirror the calculated point across all octants, reducing the loop range to pi/4.
keyPoints: Uses trigonometric functions: x = xc + r * cos(theta), y = yc + r * sin(theta).
Suffers from high computational overhead due to floating-point arithmetic and sin/cos operations.
Requires a sufficiently small angular step size to avoid gaps (aliasing) in the drawn circle.
Can be optimized using 8-way symmetry to calculate only one octant (0 to 45 degrees).
Essential conceptual stepping stone before moving to incremental rasterization algorithms like Bresenham's.
mistakes: Using too large an angular step size -> Results in dashed or dotted circles with missing pixels. Fix: Make step size inversely proportional to the radius r (e.g., 1.0 / r).
Forgetting to cast floating-point coordinates to integers -> Results in compilation errors or incorrect pixel placement. Fix: Use std::round() before plotting.
Recalculating sin and cos without optimization -> Slows down rendering. Fix: Use symmetry or incremental angle generation.
cg.circle-polar.syntax:
x = xc + r * cos(theta)
y = yc + r * sin(theta)
theory: What is the main drawback of the polar coordinate circle drawing algorithm?
It requires heavy floating-point arithmetic and slow trigonometric evaluations (sin, cos), making it inefficient.
How can the performance of the polar circle algorithm be improved?
By using 8-way symmetry to compute only 1/8th of the circle (0 to 45 degrees) and mirroring the rest.
Why do we need a dynamic step size d_theta based on the radius?
If the step size is fixed and too large, pixels will be skipped, causing gaps in the circle.
What is 8-way symmetry in circle drawing?
The property where a pixel at (x, y) in the first octant implies corresponding pixels in all other 7 octants by sign flipping and coordinate swapping.
Does C++ standard library provide the value of PI?
Yes, <cmath> provides M_PI when #define _USE_MATH_DEFINES is set prior to inclusion (standardized further in C++20/C++23 features).
Is the polar method an incremental algorithm?
No, it computes each point independently using absolute angle values rather than using previous pixel states.

cg.bresenham-circle.explain:
Bresenham's Circle Algorithm is an efficient rasterization method used to draw circles using only integer addition, subtraction, and bit-shifting operations. It avoids the costly floating-point calculations and trigonometric functions found in polar or explicit equation methods.

The algorithm evaluates a decision parameter at each step to determine whether the next pixel should move strictly horizontally or diagonally inward towards the center, keeping the rasterized path as close to the true mathematical circle as possible.

This matters immensely in computer graphics and game development for real-time rendering performance, ensuring circles render smoothly and instantly without CPU bottlenecks.

Think of walking along the perimeter of a circular track where at each step forward, you only have to check whether stepping straight or taking a diagonal step keeps you closest to the painted white line of the track boundary.
how: Initialize starting coordinates at (x = 0, y = r) and calculate the initial decision parameter: d = 3 - 2 * r.
Plot the initial symmetric points across all 8 octants for the starting position (0, r).
Loop while x <= y: check if the decision parameter d < 0.
If d < 0, the pixel is closer to the interior: update d = d + 4 * x + 6 and increment x by 1.
If d >= 0, the pixel is closer to the exterior/diagonal: update d = d + 4 * (x - y) + 10, increment x by 1, and decrement y by 1.
Plot the symmetric points for the new (x, y) coordinates at each iteration until the loop terminates.
keyPoints: Uses only fast integer arithmetic (addition, subtraction, multiplication by powers of 2).
Initial decision parameter formula: `d = 3 - 2 * r`.
Employs 8-way symmetry to draw the entire circle by calculating only one octant.
Decision update rules depend on whether `d < 0` (east pixel) or `d >= 0` (southeast pixel).
Significantly faster than trigonometric or floating-point square root approaches.
mistakes: Mixing floating-point types into decision parameter calculations -> Defeats the speed advantage of Bresenham's algorithm. Fix: Keep all decision variables and loop counters strictly as integers.
Incorrect initial decision parameter formula -> Using `d = 1 - r` (which belongs to the Midpoint circle algorithm) instead of `3 - 2 * r`. Fix: Use `3 - 2 * r` for standard Bresenham formulation.
Continuing the loop past x = y -> Causes overlapping or distorted octant plotting. Fix: Ensure loop condition is strictly `while (x <= y)`.
theory: What makes Bresenham's circle algorithm faster than analytical circle equations?
It completely eliminates floating-point arithmetic and trigonometric functions, relying entirely on integer additions and shifts.
What is the starting decision parameter for Bresenham's circle algorithm?
d = 3 - 2 * r, where r is the radius.
When does the loop terminate in Bresenham's circle algorithm?
When x exceeds y (i.e., when x > y), which marks the boundary of the first octant.
Why is 8-way symmetry applicable to circles?
Because a circle is symmetric across both X and Y axes as well as the diagonal lines y = x and y = -x.
Can Bresenham's algorithm be used for drawing ellipses?
No, ellipses require a modified midpoint or specific elliptical Bresenham variation because they lack uniform radius symmetry across all 4 quadrants.
What type of arithmetic operations are used in the update step?
Only integer addition, subtraction, and multiplication by small constants (like 4, 6, 10).

cg.midpoint-circle.explain:
The Midpoint Circle Algorithm is a rasterization technique used to draw circles by testing the midpoint between two candidate pixels to determine which one lies closer to the actual circular path.

Derived from the circle equation function `f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 - r^2`, the algorithm evaluates the midpoint `(x + 1, y - 0.5)` to see if it falls inside or outside the circle. Based on this evaluation, it selects either the East (E) pixel or the South-East (SE) pixel.

This matters because it provides an elegant, highly optimized incremental integer approach identical in performance output to Bresenham's, but derived via direct evaluation of the midpoint test function.

Think of driving a car along a mountain road where at every turning interval, you check whether the exact middle of the road fork leans toward the cliff or the mountain wall to choose your steering adjustment.
how: Set initial coordinates to (x = 0, y = r).
Calculate the initial decision parameter for the midpoint test: p = 1 - r (or 5/4 - r, simplified to 1 - r for integer math).
Plot the initial symmetric pixels across all 8 octants for (0, r).
Loop while x <= y: check if the decision parameter p < 0.
If p < 0, the midpoint is inside the circle: select East pixel, increment x by 1, and update p = p + 2 * x + 1.
If p >= 0, the midpoint is outside or on the boundary: select South-East pixel, increment x by 1, decrement y by 1, and update p = p + 2 * x - 2 * y + 1.
keyPoints: Based on the circle function evaluation: `f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 - r^2`.
Initial decision parameter: `p = 1 - r`.
Evaluates the midpoint between candidate pixels `(x + 1, y - 0.5)`.
Uses exclusively integer arithmetic, making it extremely fast for hardware implementation.
Leverages 8-way symmetry to compute only the octant from `0` to `45^\circ`.
mistakes: Confusing initial decision parameter with Bresenham -> Midpoint uses `p = 1 - r`, whereas Bresenham uses `d = 3 - 2 * r`. Fix: Use the correct formula corresponding to the chosen algorithm derivation.
Forgetting to update both x and y when p >= 0 -> Results in broken circle arcs. Fix: Decrement y and increment x simultaneously when `p >= 0`.
Using floating-point types for decision parameter `p` -> Slows down execution unnecessarily. Fix: Initialize and update `p` strictly as an integer.
theory: What is the core concept behind the Midpoint Circle Algorithm?
It tests whether the midpoint between two candidate pixels falls inside or outside the true circle boundary.
What is the formula for the initial decision parameter p in the Midpoint Circle Algorithm?
p = 1 - r (derived from 5/4 - r by dropping the fractional part for integer arithmetic).
How does the choice of pixel differ when p < 0 versus p >= 0?
When p < 0, the midpoint is inside, so we pick the East pixel. When p >= 0, the midpoint is outside/on the boundary, so we pick the South-East pixel.
Is the Midpoint Circle Algorithm restricted to integer radius values?
Yes, rasterization algorithms operate on discrete integer pixel grids.
How many octants are directly calculated before symmetry is applied?
Only one octant (typically from theta = 0 to pi/4, or x = 0 up to x = y).
What is the relationship between the Midpoint Circle algorithm and Bresenham's circle algorithm?
They produce identical pixel paths and use similar integer updates, but are derived slightly differently (Midpoint uses function evaluation at pixel midpoints, Bresenham uses error terms).

cg.scanline-fill.explain:
The Scan-line Polygon Filling algorithm is a standard computer graphics method used to fill the interior of a polygon. Instead of testing every pixel on the screen, the algorithm processes the polygon row by row (scan line by scan line).

For a given horizontal scan line, it finds all intersection points where the scan line crosses the polygon's edges. These intersection points are sorted from left to right in X-coordinate order, and pixels between pairs of intersections (even-odd rule) are filled with the chosen color.

It matters because it is significantly faster and more systematic than pixel-by-pixel seed filling, especially for complex non-convex polygons, forming the backbone of hardware rasterization.

Think of painting window blinds: you drop down row by row, and for each row, you paint only the segments that fall inside the window frame.
how: Find the minimum and maximum Y values of the polygon to determine active scan lines.
Create an Edge Table (ET) containing all non-horizontal edges sorted by their lower Y-coordinate.
Initialize an empty Active Edge Table (AET) for the current scan line.
For each scan line from Y_min to Y_max, update the AET by removing edges whose Y_max equals the current scan line and adding edges from ET starting at the current Y.
Sort the AET entries in ascending order of their current X intersection values.
Pair up the X intersections (1st with 2nd, 3rd with 4th, etc.) and fill all pixels horizontally between each pair.
keyPoints: Relies on the Edge Table (ET) and Active Edge Table (AET) for efficiency.
Uses the parity (even-odd) rule to determine inside vs. outside regions.
Complexity depends on the number of edge intersections per scan line.
Handles both convex and concave polygons correctly.
Horizontal edges are typically ignored or pre-processed because they do not cross scan lines.
mistakes:
Mistake: Failing to handle shared vertices correctly leading to pixel artifacts.
Fix: Adjust edge endpoints so shared vertices count properly as one intersection instead of two.

Mistake: Forgetting to resort the AET at every scan line after incrementing X by 1/m.
Fix: Re-sort the AET by X coordinate on every step to maintain correct pairings.

theory: What is the primary advantage of Scan-line fill over Boundary fill?
Scan-line fill does not use recursion, avoiding stack overflow issues, and can handle complex self-intersecting or multi-part polygons more predictably.
What is an Active Edge Table (AET)?
A list of edges that intersect the current scan line, updated dynamically as the scan line moves downward.
How are horizontal edges treated in standard scan-line algorithms?
Horizontal edges are usually ignored during edge table generation because they do not intersect scan lines in a way that changes parity.
What is the role of 1/m (inverse slope) in the edge table?
It calculates the new X intersection of the edge with the next scan line (X_new = X_old + 1/m).
Does the scan-line algorithm work for concave polygons?
Yes, as long as the parity rule (filling between pairs of sorted intersections) is maintained.

cg.boundary-fill.explain:
Boundary Fill and Flood Fill are seed-based region-filling algorithms commonly used in computer graphics. They start from a given interior 'seed' pixel and inspect its neighbors recursively or iteratively until the entire enclosed area is colored.

Boundary Fill continues outward until it hits a specified boundary color. Flood Fill replaces a specific target interior color with a new fill color, regardless of boundaries, until it hits pixels of a different color.

These algorithms matter because they provide an intuitive way to color enclosed regions in paint applications without calculating complex geometric intersections.

Imagine pouring colored dye inside a closed room (boundary fill): the liquid spreads outward in all directions until it hits the walls.
how: Identify a seed pixel (x, y) inside the target region.
Check the color of the current pixel.
If the pixel is neither the boundary color nor already filled, change its color to the fill color.
Recursively call or push to a stack the neighbors of the current pixel (4-connected: top, bottom, left, right; or 8-connected: including diagonals).
Repeat until all reachable interior pixels are processed.
keyPoints: 4-connected checks 4 neighbors (up, down, left, right); 8-connected checks 8 neighbors including diagonals.
Can cause stack overflow in deep recursion for large polygons due to function call overhead.
Boundary fill stops at a predefined boundary color.
Flood fill replaces an existing interior color with a new fill color.
Often implemented iteratively using a stack or queue to prevent stack overflow.
mistakes:
Mistake: Using pure recursion for large screen resolutions.
Fix: Implement using an explicit stack or queue-based breadth-first/depth-first search.

Mistake: Choosing a seed pixel that lies on the boundary.
Fix: Ensure the seed coordinate strictly lies within the interior of the region.
theory: What is the difference between 4-connected and 8-connected filling?
4-connected checks top, bottom, left, and right neighbors. 8-connected also checks the four diagonal neighbors, preventing diagonal leakage in thin boundaries.
What causes stack overflow in recursive boundary fill algorithms?
Excessive recursion depth when filling large areas, exhausting the call stack memory.
What is the difference between Boundary Fill and Flood Fill?
Boundary fill stops when it encounters a specific boundary color. Flood fill replaces an existing interior color until it hits any different color.
How can recursion-related stack overflow be prevented?
By using an explicit data structure like a stack or queue to implement an iterative fill algorithm.
What happens if the seed pixel is outside the boundary?
The algorithm may fill the entire screen outside the boundary instead of the intended inner region.

cg.viewing-pipeline.explain:
The 2-D Viewing Pipeline is the sequence of transformations and operations required to map an object defined in application coordinates (World Coordinates) onto an output display device (Device Coordinates).

The transformation goes through distinct coordinate systems: World Coordinates (WC) -> Viewing Coordinates (VC) -> Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) -> Device Coordinates (DC). The key steps involve mapping a rectangular region called the Window in world coordinates to a corresponding rectangular region called the Viewport on the output device.

This matters because it decouples the creation of graphics from the physical screen resolution, ensuring that code drawing a scene works identically across a mobile screen, a 4K monitor, or a printer.

Think of a map maker: World coordinates are the actual terrain of the earth, the Window is the specific country selected on the map, and the Viewport is the printed space on a physical sheet of paper.
how: Define the object in World Coordinates (WC).
Transform World Coordinates into Viewing Coordinates (VC) relative to a camera/view reference point.
Clip objects that fall outside the viewing window boundaries.
Map the window coordinates to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) ranging from 0 to 1 or -1 to 1.
Map NDC to actual Device Coordinates (DC) corresponding to physical screen pixels.
keyPoints: Window: A region in World Coordinates specifying what to see.
Viewport: A region on the output device specifying where to display it.
Normalization decouples device-independent coordinates from physical hardware.
Clipping eliminates primitives outside the viewing window to save rendering time.
Transformation formulas scale and translate coordinates between systems.
mistakes:
Mistake: Confusing Window (world space) with Viewport (screen space).
Fix: Remember: Window = WHAT you look at; Viewport = WHERE you look at it on screen.

Mistake: Forgetting to preserve aspect ratio during window-to-viewport mapping, leading to image distortion.

cg.window-viewport.explain:
- Window-to-Viewport Mapping is the process of transforming a 2D world-coordinate definition (the **window**) into device coordinates on the screen or output device (the **viewport**).

- In Computer Graphics, your application defines scenes in abstract, convenient units called World Coordinates (Window). However, the physical display screen has fixed pixel boundaries (Viewport). This mapping bridges that gap.

- Think of it like taking a drawing on a piece of tracing paper (the Window) and projecting it using an overhead projector onto a specific rectangular area on a classroom whiteboard (the Viewport). Scaling makes the drawing larger or smaller, and translation shifts it to the desired screen region.
how: Define the world coordinate window limits: `[xw_min, xw_max]` and `[yw_min, yw_max]`.
Define the device coordinate viewport limits: `[xv_min, xv_max]` and `[yv_min, yv_max]`.
Calculate the scaling factors along both axes: `sx = (xv_max - xv_min) / (xw_max - xw_min)` and `sy = (yv_max - yv_min) / (yw_max - yw_min)`.
Apply the normalization and scaling formula for any point `(xw, yw)` to get viewport coordinates `(xv, yv)`.
Formula: `xv = xv_min + (xw - xw_min) * sx` and `yv = yv_min + (yw - yw_min) * sy`.
keyPoints: Window resides in World Coordinate System (WCS).
Viewport resides in Screen/Device Coordinate System (DCS).
Preserves relative proportions if `sx == sy` (uniform scaling).
Essential step in the 2D viewing pipeline before rasterization.
Linear transformation combining scaling and translation.

Forgetting to invert the Y-axis if screen coordinates have origin at top-left -> Always check display coordinate system conventions.
Dividing by zero when `xw_max == xw_min` -> Validate input boundaries before calculating scale factors.

cg.point-clipping.explain:
- Point Clipping is the simplest form of geometric clipping in computer graphics, determining whether a given 2D point lies inside or outside a specified clipping window.

- It matters because rendering points outside the displayable screen or viewport wastes processing power and can cause buffer overflow or rendering artifacts.

- Think of it like checking if a dart thrown at a wall lands strictly inside a rectangular dartboard frame. If it's inside, you mark it; if it's outside, you ignore it.
how: Receive a point with coordinates `(x, y)`.
Retrieve the clipping window boundaries: `x_min`, `x_max`, `y_min`, and `y_max`.
Check if the point's X coordinate satisfies `x_min <= x <= x_max`.
Check if the point's Y coordinate satisfies `y_min <= y <= y_max`.
If both conditions hold true, keep (accept) the point; otherwise, discard (reject) it.
keyPoints: Evaluates 4 boundary inequalities simultaneously.
No intersection calculations needed (unlike line or polygon clipping).
Forms the foundation for more complex clipping algorithms.
If any single condition fails, the point is immediately rejected.
Computationally extremely lightweight.
mistakes: Using strict inequalities (`<` or `>`) instead of inclusive inequalities (`<=` or `>=`) -> Points lying precisely on the boundary edge would be incorrectly clipped.
Forgetting to check both X and Y bounds -> A point might pass the X check but fail the Y check.
Treating point clipping like line clipping and looking for slope intercepts -> Point clipping is purely a boundary membership test.
cg.point-clipping.syntax: bool isInside = (x >= x_min && x <= x_max && y >= y_min && y <= y_max);
theory: What is point clipping?
The process of determining whether a 2D point lies within a defined clipping rectangle.
How many conditions must be checked for a 2D point?
Four inequalities (left, right, bottom, and top bounds).
Is point clipping computationally expensive?
No, it only requires simple comparison operations.
What happens to a point lying exactly on the clipping boundary?
It is typically retained (accepted) since boundaries are inclusive.
Can point clipping be applied in 3D?
Yes, by adding a Z-axis check (`z_min <= z <= z_max`).

cg.cohen-sutherland.explain:
- The Cohen-Sutherland Algorithm is an efficient line-clipping method that uses 4-bit region codes to categorize line endpoints relative to a rectangular clipping window, rapidly accepting, rejecting, or splitting lines.

- It matters because clipping every single pixel of a line against screen boundaries is slow. This algorithm quickly eliminates lines completely outside the window using bitwise logic before doing heavy math.

- Think of dividing a map into a 3x3 grid around a central room (the window). Every location outside the room gets a specific 4-digit postal code (Top, Bottom, Right, Left) so you instantly know in which direction the point lies relative to the room.
how: Assign a 4-bit region code `TBRL` (Top, Bottom, Right, Left) to both endpoints of the line based on their coordinates relative to the window limits.
Triage step 1 (Trivial Accept): If both region codes are `0000`, both endpoints are inside the window. Keep the entire line.
Triage step 2 (Trivial Reject): Perform a bitwise AND (`code1 & code2`). If the result is non-zero, both points share an outside region (e.g., both are to the left). Discard the entire line.
If neither trivial condition is met, the line crosses a boundary. Pick an endpoint that is outside (`code != 0000`).
Find the intersection point of the line with the window boundary using line slope formulas, replace the outside endpoint with this intersection, and repeat the loop until the line is clipped.
keyPoints: Region code bit format: Bit 1 = Top, Bit 2 = Bottom, Bit 3 = Right, Bit 4 = Left.
Trivial acceptance condition: `code1 == 0 && code2 == 0`.
Trivial rejection condition: `(code1 & code2) != 0`.
Reduces unnecessary intersection calculations for clearly visible or hidden lines.
Works exclusively with rectangular clipping windows.
mistakes: Using bitwise OR instead of bitwise AND for trivial rejection -> Must use `code1 & code2` because a non-zero bitwise AND means *both* share an outside zone.
Forgetting to recalculate region codes after finding an intersection point -> The new endpoint must get a fresh region code before the next iteration.
Incorrect bit position mapping in code generation -> Ensure order `TBRL` is consistently followed.

const int INSIDE = 0; // 0000
const int LEFT = 1;   // 0001
const int RIGHT = 2;  // 0010
const int BOTTOM = 4; // 0100
const int TOP = 8;    // 1000

theory: What is the primary advantage of Cohen-Sutherland algorithm?
It quickly filters out lines that are completely inside or completely outside using fast bitwise operations, avoiding expensive intersection math.
How many bits are used in the region code?
4 bits, representing Top, Bottom, Right, and Left.
Explain the condition for Trivial Rejection.
`code1 & code2 != 0`. This proves both endpoints share an external region relative to the same boundary.
Can Cohen-Sutherland handle non-rectangular clipping windows?
No, it is strictly designed for rectangular clipping windows aligned with coordinate axes.
What happens if `code0 | code1 == 0`?
Both endpoints are inside the window, resulting in trivial acceptance of the entire line.

cg.cyrus-beck.explain:
The Cyrus–Beck line clipping algorithm is a general parametric line-clipping method used in computer graphics. Unlike Cohen–Sutherland which is restricted to rectangular windows, Cyrus–Beck can clip a line segment against any convex polygon (or polyhedron in 3D). It uses parametric equations of lines and the normal vectors of the clipping window edges.

The algorithm expresses a line segment using a parameter $t$ ranging from $0$ to $1$. By taking the dot product of the line points with the inward-normal vectors of the clipping boundaries, it determines where the line intersects the infinite lines defining the window boundaries. It then classifies these intersection points into potentially entering ($PE$) or potentially leaving ($PL$) categories to find the visible segment.

Think of a laser beam shining across a closed convex room. The walls of the room have inner-facing normals. As the laser passes through, it enters through some walls and leaves through others. Cyrus–Beck calculates the exact entry and exit times ($t$ parameters) so you only render the part of the laser beam that is strictly inside the room.
how: Express the line segment parametrically: $P(t) = P_0 + t(P_1 - P_0)$ for $0 \le t \le 1$.
Identify all clipping edges of the convex polygon along with their inward-facing normal vectors $N_i$.
For each edge, compute the dot product of the edge normal with the line direction vector $D = (P_1 - P_0)$, denoted as $W_i \cdot N_i$ where $W_i$ is a point on the edge.
Calculate the parametric value $t$ for each edge intersection using the formula: $t = - \frac{(P_0 - F_i) \cdot N_i}{D \cdot N_i}$, where $F_i$ is a point on edge $i$.
Classify each intersection as Potentially Entering ($PE$ when $D \cdot N_i < 0$) or Potentially Leaving ($PL$ when $D \cdot N_i > 0$).
Find the maximum $t$ among all $PE$ intersections ($t_{in}$) and the minimum $t$ among all $PL$ intersections ($t_{out}$). If $t_{in} \le t_{out}$, draw the line from $t_{in}$ to $t_{out}$.
keyPoints: Works for any convex clipping polygon in 2D and convex polyhedron in 3D.
Uses parametric line representation: $P(t) = P_0 + t(P_1 - P_0)$ with $0 \le t \le 1$.
Relies on inward-facing edge normals and dot products.
Classifies intersection points into Potentially Entering (PE) and Potentially Leaving (PL).
If $t_{in} > t_{out}$, the entire line segment is completely outside the clipping window.
mistakes: Using outward-facing normals instead of inward-facing normals (flips the sign of $PE$ and $PL$). + Fix: Always ensure normals point inside the convex polygon.
Forgetting to clamp the final $t_{in}$ and $t_{out}$ values between $0$ and $1$. + Fix: Set $t_{in} = \max(0, t_{in})$ and $t_{out} = \min(1, t_{out})$.
Applying Cyrus–Beck to a *concave* clipping window. + Fix: Cyrus–Beck only works correctly for convex windows; concave polygons must be decomposed first.
cg.cyrus-beck.syntax:
Parametric Line: P(t) = P0 + t*(P1 - P0), t in [0, 1]
Intersection t = - (P0 - Fi) . Ni / (D . Ni)
theory: What is the main advantage of Cyrus–Beck over Cohen–Sutherland?
Cyrus–Beck can clip lines against any arbitrary convex polygon, whereas Cohen–Sutherland is restricted to standard rectangular windows.
What do PE and PL stand for in Cyrus–Beck?
PE stands for Potentially Entering, and PL stands for Potentially Leaving.
What does a dot product $D \cdot N_i < 0$ signify?
It means the line direction vector is pointing opposite to the inward normal, making the intersection a Potentially Entering (PE) point.
Can Cyrus–Beck be used in 3D graphics?
Yes, it easily extends to 3D by clipping a 3D line segment against convex polyhedra using 3D plane equations and normals.
What happens if $t_{in} > t_{out}$?
It implies the line segment is completely outside the clipping window and is discarded.

cg.sutherland-hodgman.explain:
Sutherland–Hodgman is a classic polygon-clipping algorithm that clips a polygon against a single infinite window edge at a time. To clip against a complete rectangular (or convex) window, the polygon is passed successively through all four edge clippers (Left, Right, Bottom, Top).

The algorithm processes the vertices of the polygon in order, considering pairs of adjacent vertices (edge from vertex $S$ to vertex $P$). Depending on whether $S$ and $P$ are inside or outside the current clipping boundary, zero, one, or two vertices are output to form the clipped polygon for the next stage.

Imagine cutting a piece of dough with a rectangular cookie cutter. Instead of cutting all four sides at once, you take a straight knife, slice off everything on the left side of the dough, take that modified dough and slice off everything on the right side, then bottom, then top. Each step refines the polygon until only the portion inside the cookie cutter remains.
how: Start with the list of polygon vertices and take one clipping window edge (e.g., Left boundary).
Consider each pair of consecutive vertices: source vertex $S$ and current vertex $P$.
Test both $S$ and $P$ against the infinite line containing the current window edge.
Case 1 (Inside-Inside): Both $S$ and $P$ are inside. Output vertex $P$.
Case 2 (Inside-Outside): $S$ is inside, $P$ is outside. Output the intersection point of line $SP$ with the window edge.
Case 3 (Outside-Outside): Both $S$ and $P$ are outside. Output nothing.
Case 4 (Outside-Inside): $S$ is outside, $P$ is inside. Output both the intersection point and vertex $P$. Repeat for all edges.
keyPoints: Processes polygon edges one window boundary at a time sequentially.
Handles convex polygons correctly; can produce extraneous lines if applied directly to concave polygons.
Employs 4 distinct vertex output rules based on Inside/Outside status of vertex pairs ($S$ and $P$).
Output of one clipping stage becomes the input for the next edge clipping stage.
Standard algorithm taught in B.Tech CSE graphics curriculum for polygon clipping.
mistakes: Forgetting to update the vertex list between successive edge clipping passes. + Fix: Pass the output vertex array of edge $i$ as the input array for edge $i+1$.

Applying Sutherland–Hodgman to a concave polygon and expecting correct output without splitting. + Fix: Concave polygons can develop self-intersections or extraneous connecting edges; decompose them into convex parts or use Weiler-Atherton.
Incorrectly identifying the Inside/Outside status relative to the window edge. + Fix: Use the predefined boundary inequality (e.g., $x \ge x_{min}$ for left edge).
cg.sutherland-hodgman.syntax: For each of 4 edges: pass polygon vertices -> generate new vertex list based on Inside/Outside classification.
theory: What is the primary input and output of Sutherland–Hodgman?
Input is an arbitrary polygon (list of vertices), and output is a clipped polygon (new list of vertices).
Why is the polygon clipped against each window edge one by one?
It simplifies the geometric test from 2D area clipping to a series of 1D half-plane containment tests against single infinite lines.
How many cases are evaluated for each vertex pair $(S, P)$?
Four cases: Inside-Inside, Inside-Outside, Outside-Outside, and Outside-Inside.
Does Sutherland–Hodgman work for concave polygons?
It can fail or produce artifacts (extraneous lines) on concave polygons because a single edge split can wrap around incorrectly.
What algorithm should be used if the polygon is concave?
The Weiler–Atherton polygon clipping algorithm.

cg.transformations-2d.explain:
2D transformations are fundamental mathematical operations used in computer graphics to manipulate objects in a 2-dimensional Cartesian coordinate space. The core transformations include Translation (shifting position), Scaling (resizing), Rotation (spinning around a point), Reflection (flipping across an axis), and Shear (slanting shape).

To handle successive transformations efficiently and combine translation with linear transformations (scaling/rotation) using matrix multiplication, computer graphics uses **Homogeneous Coordinates**. By representing 2D points $(x, y)$ as 3-element vectors $(x, y, 1)$, all affine transformations can be unified into standard $3 \times 3$ matrix multiplication.

Imagine playing a video game where your character moves across the screen (translation), grows power-up size (scaling), and rotates when jumping (rotation). Behind the scenes, the computer is constantly multiplying the character's vertex coordinate matrices by transformation matrices 60 times a second.
how: Represent a 2D point as a homogeneous column vector: $P = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \\end{bmatrix}$.
Apply Translation by multiplying with $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & t_x \\ 0 & 1 & t_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\end{bmatrix}$.
Apply Scaling by multiplying with $\begin{bmatrix} s_x & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & s_y & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\end{bmatrix}$.
Apply Rotation by angle $\theta$ around origin with $\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\end{bmatrix}$.
Concatenate multiple transformations by multiplying their matrices together *before* applying them to the vertex vectors to save computational overhead.
keyPoints: Homogeneous coordinates introduce a third coordinate ($w = 1$) to unify translation with linear transforms.
Matrix multiplication for transformations is **non-commutative** ($A \times B \neq B \times A$).
Translation moves objects by additive offsets $(t_x, t_y)$.
Scaling resizes objects relative to the origin (multiply by $s_x, s_y$).
Rotation is counter-clockwise by default for positive angles $\theta$.
mistakes: Multiplying transformation matrices in the wrong order. + Fix: Remember that matrix multiplication reads from right to left ($P_{new} = T \times R \times S \times P_{old}$).
Forgetting the homogeneous coordinate $w = 1$, leading to dimension mismatch in matrix multiplication. + Fix: Always use $3 \times 3$ matrices for 2D affine transformations.
Scaling or rotating about the origin when the object is elsewhere, causing the object to fly off-screen. + Fix: Translate object to origin, apply scale/rotation, and translate back.

theory: What is an affine transformation?
A transformation that preserves collinearity (lines remain lines) and ratios of distances between points (e.g., translation, scaling, rotation, shear).
Why do we use homogeneous coordinates in 2D transformations?
To represent translation as matrix multiplication, allowing all transformations (translation, scaling, rotation) to be combined into a single $3 \times 3$ matrix.
Are 2D transformations commutative?
No, matrix multiplication is not commutative. The order of transformations (e.g., Rotate then Translate vs Translate then Rotate) matters significantly.
What is the 3x3 matrix for 2D Scaling?
diag(sx, sy, 1), meaning sx on top-left, sy in center, 1 in bottom-right.
How do you rotate an object about an arbitrary point $(xr, yr)$ instead of the origin?
Translate the point to the origin $(-xr, -yr)$, rotate by $\theta$, then translate back $(xr, yr)$.

cg.projections.explain:
Projections in computer graphics are mathematical techniques used to transform 3-D objects onto a 2-D viewing plane. Since computer screens are flat, we must flatten 3-D depth into 2-D coordinates. There are two primary categories: **Parallel** and **Perspective**.

`Parallel Projection` preserves relative dimensions and is widely used in engineering and architectural drafting (CAD), where accurate measurements matter more than realism. There are orthographic and oblique subtypes.

`Perspective Projection` mimics human vision and photography: objects closer to the camera appear larger, and parallel lines converge at **vanishing points**. This creates a strong sense of realism and depth.

Think of parallel projection like shining a parallel beam of light from infinity (like sunlight), casting shadows where shapes retain true sizes. Perspective projection is like looking down a long railroad track where the tracks appear to meet at a single point in the distance.
how: Define the 3-D scene coordinates and the camera/viewer position.
Choose between parallel projection (projector lines are parallel) or perspective projection (projector lines converge at a center of projection).
Set up the projection plane (view plane) where the 2-D image will be formed.
Apply the appropriate geometric transformation equations or matrix multiplication to map 3-D points (x, y, z) to 2-D screen points (xp, yp).
Pass the flattened coordinates to the rasterization pipeline for display.
keyPoints: Parallel projection preserves relative proportions; distance from the camera does not affect object size.
Perspective projection simulates depth and foreshortening, making distant objects appear smaller.
Orthographic projection is a special case of parallel projection where projectors are perpendicular to the projection plane.
Perspective projections feature one, two, or three vanishing points depending on how many axes the projection plane intersects.
Crucial for 3D game engines, CAD software, and VR rendering pipelines.
mistakes: Mistake: Using perspective projection for technical CAD drawings. Fix: Use orthographic parallel projection to maintain accurate scale and dimensions.
Mistake: Forgetting that parallel projection ignores depth scaling. Fix: Ensure z-buffering or depth sorting is handled separately if occlusion matters.
Mistake: Confusing center of projection distance with focal length improperly, causing extreme distortion. Fix: Tune the projection matrix parameters carefully.

theory: What is the main difference between parallel and perspective projection?

Parallel projection uses parallel projectors and preserves true dimensions without foreshortening. Perspective projection uses converging projectors toward a center of projection, causing distant objects to appear smaller.
What is foreshortening?
The visual effect where objects and lines appear shorter or smaller as their distance from the viewer increases.
When should you use orthographic projection?
In engineering drawings, architectural blueprints, and 2D/isometric games where precise measurement is required.
What is a vanishing point?
A point in a perspective drawing where parallel lines that are not parallel to the projection plane appear to converge.
Can parallel projection produce realistic 3D scenes?
Not typically, because humans perceive depth through perspective; parallel projection lacks depth cues like relative sizing.
What is the center of projection?
The point from which projection rays emanate in perspective projection, representing the viewer's eye or camera lens.

cg.projection-math.explain:
The mathematics of planar geometric projections relies heavily on **homogeneous coordinates** and 4x4 matrix transformations. In standard 3-D Cartesian space, perspective projections involve non-linear division by depth ($z$), which cannot be represented by a standard affine matrix multiplication alone.

By converting points to homogeneous coordinates $(X, Y, Z, W)$, we can pack the division into the matrix structure itself. When multiplied by a **projection matrix**, the $z$-coordinate is transferred into the $w$-component. After matrix multiplication, a **perspective division** step ($x' = X/W, y' = Y/W, z' = Z/W$) maps the coordinates into a normalized device coordinate (NDC) cube ranging from -1 to 1.

Think of this as a mathematical lens: the projection matrix acts as a funnel that compresses world space coordinates into a standardized bounding volume ready for clipping and rasterization.
how: Express 3-D vertices in homogeneous form as 4-element vectors: [x, y, z, 1].
Construct the appropriate 4x4 projection matrix (Orthographic or Perspective based on FOV, aspect ratio, near, and far planes).
Multiply the vertex vector by the projection matrix to transform it into clip space: V_clip = M_proj * V_view.
Perform perspective division by dividing the resulting x, y, and z components by the w component (w = -z for standard right-handed systems).
Map the resulting Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) to final screen viewport coordinates.
keyPoints: Homogeneous coordinates allow perspective transformations to be expressed as linear matrix multiplications.
Perspective division is the critical step where W is divided out to achieve foreshortening.
The view volume for perspective projection is a truncated pyramid (frustum); for orthographic it is a rectangular box.
Near and far clipping planes prevent division by zero and handle depth buffer precision.
Vanishing points emerge naturally from the matrix division when lines extend to infinity.
mistakes: Mistake: Forgetting to perform perspective division after applying the projection matrix. Fix: Always divide x, y, z by w before viewport mapping.
Mistake: Incorrect near/far plane values (e.g., near = 0). Fix: Near plane must always be a positive non-zero value to prevent division by zero.
Mistake: Mixing up row-major and column-major matrix conventions in OpenGL vs DirectX. Fix: Verify matrix multiplication order (v' = M * v vs v' = v * M).
cg.projection-math.syntax:

Perspective Division: x_ndc = X / W, y_ndc = Y / W
theory: Why do we use homogeneous coordinates in 3D computer graphics?
They allow translation and perspective projections to be represented as standard matrix multiplications combined with linear algebra.
What is the role of the W component after projection matrix multiplication?
W holds the depth value (-z), which is used during perspective division to scale coordinates for foreshortening.
What is a view frustum?
The truncated pyramid volume in 3D space that defines what objects are visible to the camera.
Why must the near clipping plane be greater than zero?
To avoid division by zero errors during perspective division when z approaches the camera origin.
What are Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC)?
A standardized coordinate cube ranging from -1 to 1 across x, y, and z axes, independent of screen resolution.
How does an orthographic projection matrix differ from a perspective matrix?
Orthographic matrices use parallel rays and do not alter W (keeps W=1), eliminating perspective division scaling.

cg.coordinate-systems.explain:
In 3-D computer graphics rendering, an object travels through a sequence of **coordinate systems** (or spaces) before it finally appears on your monitor. Each space uses its own origin and units, and matrices are used to convert coordinates from one space to the next.

1. `Local/Model Space`: The object's own internal coordinate system (e.g., a car centered at origin `(0,0,0)`).
2. `World Space`: Placing multiple objects into a shared global scene.
3. `View/Eye Space`: Transforming the scene relative to the camera's position and orientation.
4. `Clip Space`: Applying projection matrices so vertices outside the view frustum are clipped.
5. `Screen/Viewport Space`: Mapping the final NDC coordinates to actual pixel locations on the display.

Imagine shooting a movie: Model space is the actor rehearsing alone in their dressing room. World space is the actor placed onto the Hollywood set. View space is the camera crew's perspective looking through the camera lens.
how: Define object geometry in Model Space using local vertex buffers.
Apply the **Model Matrix** (translation, rotation, scaling) to convert Model Space to World Space.
Apply the **View Matrix** (camera position and look-at orientation) to convert World Space to View/Eye Space.
Apply the **Projection Matrix** to transform View Space into Clip Space.
Perform perspective division and viewport transformation to convert Clip Space into Screen Pixel Space.
keyPoints: The rendering pipeline pipeline order is: Model -> World -> View -> Clip -> Screen.
Model matrix handles object transformations; View matrix handles camera movement.
World and View matrices are often combined into a single Model-View matrix in older pipelines.
Clip space prepares coordinates for clipping against the view volume boundaries.
Screen space converts normalized device coordinates into discrete pixel integers.
mistakes: Mistake: Applying the view matrix before the model matrix. Fix: Matrices are right-multiplied by vectors, so order matters (Projection * View * Model * Vertex).
Mistake: Confusing world coordinates with screen pixel coordinates. Fix: Remember world space is floating-point 3D space, screen space is 2D integer pixels.
Mistake: Forgetting to normalize normals when non-uniform scaling is applied in model space. Fix: Use the transpose of the inverse model matrix for normals.

cg.homogeneous.explain:
In 2D computer graphics, points are represented as coordinates `(x, y)`. However, standard 2D translation is an addition operation (`x' = x + t_x`), whereas scaling and rotation are multiplication operations (`x' = x * s_x`). Mixing addition and matrix multiplication makes chaining multiple transformations complex and computationally expensive.

Homogeneous coordinates solve this by representing a 2D point `(x, y)` as a 3D vector `(x, y, 1)` and a 3D point as `(x, y, z, 1)`. By adding an extra coordinate `w` (usually set to 1), translation can be expressed as a matrix multiplication using a 3×3 matrix (for 2D) or a 4×4 matrix (for 3D).

This matters because it unifies all affine transformations—translation, scaling, rotation, and shearing—into a single matrix multiplication framework, which is crucial for hardware acceleration on GPUs.

Think of it like adding a depth dimension to a flat sheet of paper. By lifting the points slightly off the paper into 3D space (`w=1`), we can slide the entire paper around using a simple tilt or shift matrix, and then project it back down.
how: Take a standard 2D point coordinate represented as an ordered pair (x, y).
Append a third coordinate, w, setting its initial value to 1, resulting in the column vector [x, y, 1]^T.
Construct a 3x3 transformation matrix where the bottom row is [0, 0, 1] and the upper-left 2x2 submatrix handles scaling/rotation, while the rightmost column handles translation.
Multiply the 3x3 transformation matrix by the 3x1 homogeneous coordinate vector to get the transformed vector [x', y', w']^T.
Convert back to Cartesian coordinates by dividing x' and y' by w' if w' != 1.
keyPoints: Homogeneous coordinates represent an n-dimensional point using n+1 coordinates.
Enables combination of rotation, scaling, and translation using pure matrix multiplication.
For 2D transformations, matrices are 3×3; for 3D transformations, matrices are 4×4.
The extra coordinate w is typically 1 for points and 0 for vectors (vectors are immune to translation).
Division by w is required during perspective projection transformations.
mistakes: Forgetting to set w = 1 for point coordinates, leading to incorrect transformation results. Always initialize points as (x, y, 1).
Applying translation vectors with w = 1 instead of w = 0. Vectors should have w = 0 so they do not translate.
Multiplying matrices in the wrong order. Matrix multiplication is not commutative.
Forgetting to perform perspective division (dividing by w) when rendering 3D scenes.
theory: What are homogeneous coordinates?
A coordinate system where an n-dimensional point is represented by n+1 variables, allowing translations to be expressed as matrix multiplications.
Why is the third coordinate 'w' usually set to 1 for points?
To ensure that after matrix multiplication, the affine properties are preserved, and division by w yields the correct 2D Cartesian coordinates.
How do you represent a vector versus a point in homogeneous coordinates?
A point has w = 1 (subject to translation), while a direction vector has w = 0 (unaffected by translation).
Why can't standard 2D Cartesian coordinates handle translation with matrix multiplication alone?
Because translation is an additive operation (x + tx), whereas matrix transformation relies on linear combinations (multiplication and addition).
What is the bottom row of a standard 2D affine transformation matrix in homogeneous form?
Always [0, 0, 1].

cg.composite.explain:
In computer graphics, complex animations and object placements rarely involve just a single transformation. An object might need to be scaled, rotated around its own center, and then translated to a specific position in the world. 

Composite transformations refer to the process of combining multiple individual transformation matrices (like translation, scaling, and rotation) into a single resultant matrix via matrix multiplication. 

This matters greatly for performance. Instead of multiplying every single vertex of a 3D model by 5 separate matrices sequentially, we pre-multiply the matrices together once to get a single composite matrix, and then multiply the vertices only once.

Think of it like following a recipe: if you need to double the flour (scale), mix it clockwise (rotate), and pour it into a pan on the top shelf (translate), you can combine these instructions into a single composite action plan before executing them on the ingredients.
how: Identify the sequence of individual transformations required (e.g., Translate, then Rotate, then Scale).
Write down the homogeneous transformation matrix for each individual step.
Multiply the matrices in the correct order. Note: Matrix multiplication is applied from right to left in column-vector notation (i.e., `P' = T * R * S * P`).
Compute the single composite matrix `M_comp = T * R * S` once.
Apply the composite matrix `M_comp` to all vertices of the object to get the final transformed coordinates efficiently.
keyPoints: Matrix multiplication order is critical: `A * B != B * A` (non-commutative).
Transformations are applied from right to left when using column vectors: `M_final = T * R * S` means Scale happens first, then Rotate, then Translate.
Pre-multiplying matrices saves massive CPU/GPU cycles for models with thousands of vertices.
Arbitrary point rotation requires translating the point to the origin, rotating, and translating back.
Composite transformations form the backbone of hierarchical modeling (scene graphs).
mistakes: Multiplying matrices from left to right assuming order doesn't matter. The rightmost matrix always acts on the original point first.
Applying rotation before translation when rotating an object about an arbitrary point (resulting in rotation around the world origin instead).
Forgetting that scaling about a fixed point requires a 3-step composite operation.
Inverting matrix multiplication order when converting from row-vector convention to column-vector convention.
cg.composite.syntax:

P_final = M_composite * P_original

Because matrix multiplication is not commutative; changing the order changes the final geometric outcome.

1. Translate object so (xr, yr) is at the origin (-xr, -yr). 2. Rotate by angle theta. 3. Translate back (+xr, +yr).
What is the advantage of composite transformations?
Reduces computational overhead by combining multiple transformation matrices into a single matrix before applying to vertices.
If we apply T(1,2) then R(90) to a point, which operation executes first geometrically?
Rotation R(90) executes first, followed by Translation T(1,2) (right-to-left evaluation).
Can two successive translations be combined? What is their property?
Yes, T(x1, y1) * T(x2, y2) = T(x1+x2, y1+y2). Translations are commutative with each other.

cg.transformations-3d.explain:
In 3D computer graphics, objects exist in a three-dimensional space with `X`, `Y`, and `Z` axes. To manipulate these objects (move them, resize them, or spin them around any axis), we extend our homogeneous coordinate system from 3×3 matrices to 4×4 matrices. A 3D point is represented as a 4-element column vector `(x, y, z, 1)`.

Unlike 2D rotation where rotation is strictly around the origin in the Z-plane, 3D rotation can happen independently around the X-axis, Y-axis, Z-axis, or any arbitrary axis. Each of these requires dedicated rotation matrices.

This matters because every modern video game, CAD software, and CGI movie relies entirely on 4x4 matrix pipelines to project 3D worlds onto 2D computer screens.

Think of a robotic arm in a factory: the base rotates on the Y-axis, the elbow pitches on the X-axis, and the wrist rolls on the Z-axis. Computing the final claw position requires chaining these 4x4 spatial transformation matrices together.
how: Represent any 3D vertex as a 4x1 homogeneous column vector: [x, y, z, 1]^T.
Use a 4x4 identity matrix as the starting point for any transformation sequence.
Apply 3D Translation by placing translation values (tx, ty, tz) in the rightmost column of the 4x4 matrix.
Apply 3D Scaling by placing scaling factors (sx, sy, sz) along the main diagonal of the 4x4 matrix.
Apply 3D Rotation by using trigonometric functions (sin, cos) in specific submatrices depending on whether rotating around the X, Y, or Z axis.
keyPoints: 3D transformations use 4×4 matrices and 4-element homogeneous vectors `(x, y, z, 1)`.
Rotation around the X-axis keeps the X coordinate constant while modifying Y and Z.
Rotation around the Y-axis keeps the Y coordinate constant while modifying X and Z.
Rotation around the Z-axis keeps the Z coordinate constant while modifying X and Y.
Order of multiplication matters heavily in 3D rotations (Gimbal lock can occur if rotations are applied sequentially without care).
mistakes: Using 3x3 matrices for 3D graphics operations, which makes translation impossible to include.
Confusing the sign of the sine term in rotation matrices (e.g., mixing up the signs for Y-axis rotation versus X and Z axes).
Forgetting to include the bottom row [0, 0, 0, 1] in 4x4 transformation matrices.
Applying rotations in the wrong sequence when combining Euler angles.
theory: Why do we need 4x4 matrices for 3D transformations?
Because 3D homogeneous coordinates require a 4-element vector (x, y, z, 1), necessitating a 4x4 matrix to perform linear transformations and translations.
What does the Y-axis rotation matrix look like?
It leaves the Y row and column as [0, 1, 0] with cos and -sin/sin distributed across X and Z coordinates.
What is Gimbal Lock?
A loss of one degree of freedom in 3-dimensional space that occurs when the axes of two orthogonal gimbals are driven into a parallel configuration.
How is 3D scaling represented in a 4x4 matrix?
Diagonal elements M[0][0]=sx, M[1][1]=sy, M[2][2]=sz, with M[3][3]=1.
Are 3D rotations commutative?
No, rotating around X then Y yields a completely different result than rotating around Y then X.

cg.hidden-surface.explain:
Hidden Surface Removal (HSR), also known as hidden surface elimination or visible surface determination, is a fundamental process in computer graphics where objects or parts of objects that are obscured by other closer objects from the viewer's perspective are removed before rendering.

It matters immensely because in a 3D scene, rendering every polygon regardless of its position wastes massive computational power and causes visual confusion by drawing back-facing or occluded elements on top of closer ones.

Think of it like looking out a window: you can see the tree in your yard, but you cannot see the house behind the tree because the tree blocks your line of sight. HSR algorithms calculate this exact line-of-sight obstruction for every pixel on the screen.
how: Transform all 3D scene objects from world coordinates to the viewer's 3D projection coordinate system.
Perform back-face culling to eliminate polygons pointing away from the camera, reducing the workload.
Apply spatial sorting or depth testing algorithms (like Z-buffer or Scan-line) to resolve overlapping surfaces.
Render only the surviving visible pixel fragments onto the 2D frame buffer.
keyPoints: HSR algorithms are categorized into object-space methods (done in vector/geometric precision) and image-space methods (done at pixel resolution).
Back-face culling is a quick preliminary HSR test using the normal vector dot product with the view vector: $V \cdot N > 0$.
Object-space methods are resolution-independent but computationally complex for dense polygon meshes.
Image-space methods (like Z-buffering) scale with screen resolution rather than scene complexity.
mistakes: Confusing object-space and image-space methods; remember object-space works with exact geometry, while image-space works on the discrete pixel grid.
Failing to clip objects outside the view frustum before performing HSR, leading to wasted processing.
Ignoring precision issues like Z-fighting when two coplanar surfaces share identical depth values.

theory: What is the difference between object-space and image-space hidden surface removal?
Object-space methods compare objects against each other using exact mathematical coordinates, while image-space methods determine visibility at each pixel location on the display screen.
What is back-face culling?
A technique that removes polygons whose normal vectors point away from the viewer, assuming the object is a closed solid polyhedron.
Why is hidden surface removal necessary in computer graphics?
To avoid rendering objects that are blocked from view, saving GPU resources and maintaining correct depth perception.
What is depth precision artifact or Z-fighting?
Flickering or visual corruption that occurs when two surfaces have nearly identical depth values, causing the depth buffer to alternate which one is closer.
Name two classic image-space algorithms for HSR.
Z-buffer (Depth Buffer) algorithm and Scan-line algorithm.

cg.z-buffer.explain:
The Z-buffer (or depth buffer) algorithm is an image-space approach used in computer graphics to manage image depth coordinates in 3D rendering. It associates a depth value (Z) with every pixel on the screen, typically initialized to the maximum possible depth (farthest away).

It matters because it provides an efficient, per-pixel way to solve the hidden surface problem without needing to sort complex polygons globally. It allows arbitrary intersecting, moving, or complex geometry to be rendered correctly.

Imagine stacking sheets of transparent paper on a table; as you draw items, you only keep the ink from the stroke that lands closest to your eye on each specific coordinate grid square, discarding anything that falls underneath.
how: Initialize the color buffer to background color and the Z-buffer (depth buffer) to maximum depth (e.g., 1.0 or infinity).
Rasterize each polygon in the scene into individual pixels.
For each generated pixel of a polygon, calculate its depth (Z) relative to the viewer.
Compare the calculated Z with the current value stored in the Z-buffer at that pixel's (x, y) coordinate.
If the new pixel's Z is closer than the stored Z, update the frame buffer with the new color and update the Z-buffer with the new Z value.
keyPoints: Operates in image-space, meaning its performance depends on screen resolution and fragment count rather than polygon count.
Requires two main memory buffers: the frame buffer (for color) and the depth buffer (for Z values).
Modern GPUs implement Z-buffering in dedicated hardware with hierarchical depth tests for optimization.
Does not handle transparent surfaces correctly without modifications (like order-independent transparency).
mistakes: Forgetting to initialize the Z-buffer to the maximum depth value before rendering a new frame.
Mixing up near and far clipping plane values, resulting in inverted depth tests where background objects occlude foreground ones.
Assuming Z-buffer precision is linear; standard Z-buffers are non-linear (hyperbolic), offering high precision near the camera and low precision far away.

cg.scanline-hsr.explain:
The Scan-line algorithm for Hidden Surface Removal is an image-space visibility determination technique that processes an image one horizontal scan line at a time, rather than processing polygon by polygon or pixel by pixel independently.

It matters because it exploits coherence—the property that adjacent pixels and scan lines share similar color and depth characteristics—making it faster and more memory-efficient than a naive pixel-by-pixel Z-buffer approach in certain architectures.

Imagine reading a printed page line by line from top to bottom; as you track across a single line, you note which words (polygons) overlap and only write down the letters that are currently visible on that exact line before moving to the next line down.
how: Sort all polygon edges into an Edge Table (ET) sorted by their minimum Y coordinate.
Maintain an Active Edge Table (AET) containing edges that intersect the current scan line.
As the scan line moves down, update the AET by adding new edges and removing edges that terminate.
Use span coherence to determine which polygon spans across intervals on the current scan line and calculate their depths.
Output the color of the polygon with the minimum depth (closest to the viewer) for each span on the scan line.
keyPoints: Combines image-space and object-space concepts by utilizing polygon edge tables sorted in object space and evaluating them per scan line.
Significantly reduces calculations by taking advantage of scan-line and span coherence.
Efficiently handles intersecting polygons by subdividing spans when depth order changes along a scan line.
Requires polygon sorting along the Y-axis as a preprocessing step.
mistakes: Confusing scan-line rendering with ray tracing; scan-line operates directly on projected polygon edges and spans.

cg.area-subdivision.explain:
Area Subdivision, famously implemented as the **Warnock algorithm**, is a hidden-surface removal technique in computer graphics that uses a divide-and-conquer strategy. It operates in image space by examining the bounding box of the entire screen (or viewport) and checking its relationship with all polygon surfaces in the scene. If the area is too complex—meaning multiple polygons overlap, intersect, or obscure each other—the region is recursively subdivided into four equal quadrants. This process continues until each sub-region is simple enough to be resolved easily (e.g., zero polygons, one enclosing polygon, or a single polygon covering the entire region).

This algorithm matters because it elegantly handles complex overlapping geometries without requiring a full, pixel-by-pixel Z-buffer depth sort across the entire high-resolution frame simultaneously. It focuses computational effort only where visual complexity actually exists.

Think of it like sorting a massive pile of mixed papers on a large table. Instead of sorting every single overlapping sheet across the entire table all at once, you divide the table into four quadrants. If a quadrant has just one clean sheet or is completely empty, you finish it instantly. If a quadrant still has a messy pile of overlapping papers, you divide that specific quadrant into four smaller sub-sections and repeat until every small section is trivial to sort.
how: Initialize the algorithm with the entire screen or viewport area as the initial window.
Determine the relationship between each polygon and the current viewing area (e.g., completely outside, completely inside, intersecting, or containing the area).
Check for simplicity conditions: if zero polygons affect the area, shade it background color; if one polygon surrounds the area, display it; if the area is a single pixel, compute the closest depth.
If the area is still too complex and greater than a single pixel, subdivide the rectangular viewing area into four equal quadrants.
Recursively apply the same tests and subdivision steps to each of the four quadrants until all regions satisfy simplicity conditions.
keyPoints: Warnock's algorithm is an image-space hidden-surface removal method.
Uses a recursive divide-and-conquer approach based on screen areas.
Terminates subdivision when the region reaches single-pixel size or meets basic simplicity criteria.
Handles polygon intersections and cyclic overlaps naturally.
Computationally expensive for real-time applications due to recursive overhead, historically important for ray casting and precision rendering.
mistakes:
Mistake: Forgetting to handle polygons that completely enclose the view area. 
Fix: Ensure your test checks if a single polygon entirely covers the region, allowing immediate rendering without further subdivision.

Mistake: Infinite recursion when reaching sub-pixel dimensions. 
Fix: Always enforce a base case where recursion stops when the region size equals 1x1 pixel.
